passage: In the village near Thanjavur, Shalini, twenty-five, carried the clay pot around Rukmini Paati's pyre three times, because Paati had asked for her and no one else. Some relatives murmured; her uncle hushed them. Shalini's hands knew the steps from the priest's instructions, but her face felt made of wood. She didn't cry at the cremation ground, and wondered what was wrong with her. That night, sorting Paati's saris, she found the green one Paati had worn to her graduation, still smelling of coconut oil. Shalini sat on the floor and sobbed. Her mother didn't tell her to be strong. She just sat down beside her and held her until it passed.

qa.q: How many times did Shalini carry the pot around the pyre?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling at the cremation ground?
qa.a: Shalini felt numb, her face 'made of wood', and worried that not crying meant something was wrong.

qa.q: What did Shalini's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She didn't tell Shalini to be strong; she sat beside her and held her, letting her cry as long as she needed.

qa.q: How might Shalini's uncle have felt when he hushed the murmuring relatives?
qa.a: He likely felt protective of Shalini and respectful of Paati's wish, wanting the rites done in peace.

grounding: Shows a young adult performing last rites for a grandparent who feels duty and numbness first and grief later, and who is allowed to cry.

passage: On the first day of shiva in their Haifa apartment, Noa, twenty-four, sat on the low chair in the shirt she had torn at the graveside for Saba. She had said the prayer, shovelled earth onto the coffin and greeted every visitor. She felt nothing at all, as if watching herself through glass. On the third afternoon her friend Leila came with a pot of lentil soup, sat beside her and said, 'You don't have to be the host. Tell me about him.' Noa started with Saba's terrible jokes and ended with her face in Leila's shoulder, crying so hard she shook. Leila didn't hush her. The mirrors stayed covered; the soup went cold. Neither of them minded.

qa.q: What did Leila bring?
qa.a: A pot of lentil soup.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling during the first days of shiva?
qa.a: Noa felt numb and detached, 'as if watching herself through glass', while doing every duty correctly.

qa.q: Why did Leila's visit help Noa?
qa.a: Leila freed her from hosting, asked about Saba and let her cry without hushing, giving grief room alongside the rituals.

qa.q: How might Leila have felt holding Noa as she cried?
qa.a: Leila probably felt sad and tender, glad to be trusted with Noa's grief.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult mourning a grandparent through the rituals, feeling grief, duty and numbness at once, and finding that being allowed to cry matters as much as the tasks.

passage:
Hospice care note, Room 4 — family support

Mr Rahman passed away at 5:10 this morning. His grandson Asif, 24, had sat with him through the night.

Asif was calm and very organised afterwards. He called the family, spoke to the masjid about the ghusl and the janaza, signed the forms, and asked me twice whether he had done everything correctly. He did not cry. His hands were steady; his voice was flat.

When his mother, Farida, arrived, she held his face and said, "You don't have to be strong right now, beta. You can do the duties and still cry." He sat down on the chair by the window and wept for a long time. She held him.

What I did next: I gave them the room, brought water, and told Asif that numbness is a common part of grief and that our counsellor can meet him after the burial if he wants.

qa.q: What time did Mr Rahman pass away?
qa.a: Mr Rahman passed away at 5:10 this morning.

qa.q: What did Asif's steady hands and flat voice suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Asif was probably numb with grief, holding it back by focusing on the duties and doing them correctly.

qa.q: Which responses helped Asif, and why?
qa.a: Farida telling him he could do the duties and still cry, and the carer giving them privacy and offering the counsellor; both let grief come alongside duty.

qa.q: What might Farida have felt seeing her son so composed?
qa.a: Farida likely felt worried and tender, sensing he was holding his grief in, and wanted to let him release it.

grounding: Shows a young adult handling a grandparent's last rites with numb efficiency, and being given permission to cry as well as do the duties.

passage:
Wednesday night.

Today I lit Aaji's pyre. The priest hesitated when Baba said it would be me, since there are no grandsons. Baba said, "She was Aaji's shadow for twenty-five years. It's her." So it was me.

I kept waiting to feel something. I walked the rounds with the pot, held the torch, repeated the words. My hands knew what to do. My heart felt wrapped in cotton.

Zubin stood at the back the whole time. He isn't Hindu and didn't know any of it, but he didn't leave.

It was only at home, when I opened her steel cupboard and smelled her talcum powder, that I sat on the floor and cried until my ribs hurt. Aai came and sat with me and didn't say anything.

I did the rites right. I'm glad I also got to cry.

Damini

qa.q: Why did the priest hesitate?
qa.a: The priest hesitated because there are no grandsons and Baba said it would be Damini.

qa.q: How did Damini feel while performing the rites?
qa.a: Damini felt numb, the heart as if wrapped in cotton, even as her hands knew what to do.

qa.q: What helped Damini hold both duty and grief?
qa.a: Doing the rites carefully, then being allowed to cry at home with Aai sitting beside her, without anyone rushing her.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt standing at the back?
qa.a: Zubin may have felt out of place, not knowing the rituals, yet steady in wanting to be there for Damini.

grounding: Shows a young adult performing a grandparent's last rites while numb, and finding that being able to cry matters as much as doing the tasks right.

passage:
Salma: how did it go today? thinking of you
Joseph: it's done. I carried the coffin with my cousins
Joseph: read the passage Appachan liked. didn't mess it up
Salma: that's a lot to do in one day
Joseph: everyone keeps saying I was so strong
Joseph: honestly I felt nothing. just kept doing the next thing
Salma: that happens. grief isn't always tears right away
Joseph: then at the cemetery Ammachi held my hand and I couldn't stop crying. in front of everyone
Salma: good. you're allowed. he was your Appachan
Joseph: I thought I had to hold it together for the family
Salma: you did the duties. you can also be sad. both
Joseph: can you call me
Salma: I'll call tonight. and tomorrow

qa.q: What did Joseph read at the funeral?
qa.a: Joseph read the passage Appachan liked.

qa.q: How was Joseph feeling during the day's duties?
qa.a: Joseph felt numb, doing the next thing without feeling anything, until grief broke through at the cemetery.

qa.q: How did Salma support Joseph?
qa.a: She checked in, said that numbness and tears are both part of grief, said crying was allowed, and offered to call that night.

qa.q: What might Ammachi have felt when she held Joseph's hand?
qa.a: Ammachi likely felt her own grief and a wish to comfort her grandchild, sharing the loss.

grounding: Shows a young adult carrying out a grandparent's funeral duties while numb, then crying, and a friend affirming that duty and grief can coexist.

passage:
In the village near Bardhaman, Kamal, twenty-five, stood by the pyre on the riverbank, holding the burning stick. Dadu was gone. The priest told him what to do and he did it: walk round, touch the flame to the wood, pour the ghee. He felt nothing, only a strange hollow calm, as if watching someone else. Relatives murmured that he was being strong.
His college friend Tanvir had taken two buses from Kolkata to be there. He stood a step behind Kamal the whole time, not speaking.
Later, when the smoke rose, Kamal saw Dadu's old reading glasses in his uncle's hand. His legs gave way. He sat on the wet sand and sobbed like a child. An aunt moved to hush him; Tanvir put a hand on his shoulder instead, and the aunt stepped back. Kamal cried until the fire was low. Then he got up and finished the rites.

qa.q: What did Kamal see in his uncle's hand?
qa.a: Dadu's old reading glasses.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel while performing the rites at first?
qa.a: He felt numb and hollow, calm as if he were watching someone else.

qa.q: Why was it important that Kamal was allowed to cry?
qa.a: Crying let his grief come out alongside the duty, so he could finish the rites as himself rather than only being strong.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt standing behind Kamal?
qa.a: Tanvir probably felt sad and protective, wanting to support his friend quietly without intruding on the ritual.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult performing a grandparent's last rites who feels grief, duty and numbness, and is allowed to cry.
